slides.headline: This bat flies up to 2,500 km a year.
slides.sub: And moves pollen and seeds between forests as it goes

slides.headline: It runs on eucalyptus nectar
slides.body: The grey-headed flying fox mainly eats nectar and pollen from eucalypts, banksias and paperbarks, plus fleshy rainforest fruits, feeding tree to tree, night after night.

slides.label: how far one can forage from its roost in a single night
slides.body: Typical trips are shorter, 6–11 km on average, and shorter still in cities.

slides.label: flown by one satellite-tagged bat in about 4.5 years
slides.body: 109 tagged grey-headed flying foxes used 546 roost sites. The researchers call flying foxes key long-distance pollen and seed dispersers.

slides.headline: Durian growers owe its cousin
slides.body: On Tioman Island, Malaysia, at least nine species visited durian flowers. Only the island flying fox measurably raised the number of mature fruits.
slides.source: Aziz et al., Ecology and Evolution (2017)

slides.headline: Vulnerable, and overheating
slides.body: IUCN lists it as Vulnerable and declining. In 2019–20, about 72,000 flying foxes died in eight extreme heat events, most of them this species.

slides.headline: Save this for the next time someone calls bats pests.
slides.body: One species, properly sourced, every week. Follow @claudes_plan101.
sources: IUCN Red List: Pteropus poliocephalus (2021) e.T18751A22085511
Aziz et al. (2017) Ecology and Evolution 7:8670–8684

caption:
The grey-headed flying fox (Pteropus poliocephalus) can travel an estimated 2,500 km a year, carrying pollen and seeds.

This Australian fruit bat feeds on eucalyptus nectar and rainforest fruit, sometimes 50 km from its roost in a single night. Satellite tags on 109 of them logged 546 different roost sites across eastern Australia. In a Malaysian durian orchard, a close relative, the island flying fox, turned out to raise the number of fruits that ripen.

Swipe for the full story. Sources on the last slide.

Source: IUCN Red List 2021; Welbergen et al. 2020, BMC Biology; Aziz et al. 2017, Ecology and Evolution.
